titre: The Citicorp Center's Engineer Hid That He Had Nearly Brought It Down
accroche: In 1978, William LeMessurier discovers that a quartering wind could make the tower he has just built in Manhattan collapse.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1977, the Citicorp Center opens in Manhattan, a fifty-nine-story skyscraper set on four columns that are not at its corners. They sit at the center of each of its sides, to free up the corner where a church was to be rebuilt. To carry wind loads toward these columns, the engineer William LeMessurier designed diagonal chevron braces, backed by a tuned mass damper installed on the roof, a world first for stabilizing a building this way.

## Two Students and a Phone Call

In May 1978, while working on a nearby project, LeMessurier learns almost by chance that a change has been made on his own construction site without his being told: to save money, the welded joints he had specified for the chevrons have been replaced by bolted joints. At the same time, a Princeton student, Diane Hartley, is devoting her thesis to the Citicorp Center and calculates that quartering winds, those that strike a corner of the building rather than a whole face, produce stresses greater than those used by LeMessurier's office; an architecture student himself questions him by phone on that same point, almost at the same time and without knowing it.

On July 24, 1978, LeMessurier reworks his calculations. He finds that, for half the floors, quartering winds increase the wind load by 40% and the stress on the now-bolted joints by 160%. A wind-tunnel testing specialist, consulted two days later, confirms and even worsens his estimates. With the damper working, a wind capable of bringing the tower down has a one-in-fifty-five chance of occurring in a given year. But the damper depends on electricity: in a power outage, a frequent occurrence during storms, that probability falls to one in sixteen.

LeMessurier warns the architect's lawyers, then Citicorp's, before convincing the bank's president himself. Welded steel plates, nicknamed “Band-Aids” by the construction crew, reinforce each critical joint, at night, sealed off behind plywood partitions while the offices operate normally by day. The city secretly prepares an evacuation plan for a ten-block area, a backup generator is installed for the damper, and Hurricane Ella threatens New York in the middle of the repair before changing course. None of this will be made public before a New Yorker article in 1995.

## What This Shifts

The story of the Citicorp Center is that of an engineer who chose, seventeen years before anyone knew, to redo his calculations rather than protect his reputation, at real risk of losing it. A more recent reassessment, carried out with tools LeMessurier did not have in 1978, has since suggested that the real danger may have been smaller than what he estimated. But at the moment he had to decide, LeMessurier had only his own calculations, and it is on those alone that he chose to act.

repere.texte: According to the calculations William LeMessurier made in late July 1978, withdrawn to his summer home in Maine after consulting a wind-tunnel testing specialist, a quartering wind capable of making the Citicorp Center collapse had a one-in-sixteen chance of occurring each year if the roof damper lost its electricity, a risk that no one outside his own office knew about until a New Yorker article published seventeen years later.
repere.source: Wikipedia (en), “Citicorp Center engineering crisis,” based on The New Yorker, May 29, 1995

carte.punch: An engineer discovers that his skyscraper has a one-in-sixteen chance of falling, and keeps it secret.
carte.idee: In 1978, the engineer William LeMessurier discovers that a construction-site change makes the Citicorp Center vulnerable to quartering winds, with a one-in-sixteen chance each year of collapsing during a power failure. He has it repaired in secret, at night, revealing nothing before 1995.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full account of the discovery and the repair, with a separate study devoted to Diane Hartley's thesis.

quiz.question: Why, according to William LeMessurier's 1978 calculations, did the Citicorp Center end up with a one-in-sixteen chance of collapsing each year?
choix: The New York ground beneath the tower had proved less stable than expected in the initial geological surveys
The damper installed on the roof had been poorly tuned from its commissioning by the company that made it
A manufacturing defect affected the steel used for the tower's four load-bearing columns
Welded joints specified by LeMessurier had been replaced by bolted joints, inadequate against quartering winds
quiz.explication: LeMessurier discovered that the bolted joints, substituted without his approval for the welded joints he had specified, did not resist quartering winds enough, those that strike a corner of the building rather than a whole face. Neither the ground, nor the damper itself, nor a defect in the columns was at fault.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why were the Citicorp Center's four columns placed at the center of each side rather than at its corners?
choix: To reduce the total amount of steel needed for the structure
To free the corner of the building where a church was to be rebuilt
To improve the view from the corner offices on the top floor
To comply with a zoning rule limiting facade height
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the columns were moved to the center of each side precisely to free the corner where a church was to be rebuilt.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who, outside LeMessurier's office, had independently spotted the building's vulnerability to quartering winds?
choix: A Princeton student, Diane Hartley, in her university thesis
A city inspector in charge of a routine safety audit
Citicorp's board of directors during a budget review
A journalist investigating the construction's cost overruns
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Diane Hartley, a Princeton student, had calculated for her thesis that quartering winds produced stresses greater than those used by LeMessurier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to the Citicorp Center's annual probability of collapse if the roof damper lost its electrical power?
choix: It stayed unchanged, the damper having no effect on this risk
It fell to zero, the structure becoming stiffer without it
It went from one in fifty-five to one in sixteen
It applied only in the winter months, outside storm season
quiz_supplementaire.explication: With the damper working, the annual risk was one in fifty-five; in a power outage, frequent during storms, it rose to one in sixteen.
